sampling.note: Label-free uniform sample; fraud count is random. Strictest option for leakage audits.

rule_description: Flag if 2+ points from: type in ['TRANSFER', 'CASH_OUT']; amount >= 200,000; amount >= 1,000,000.

ci.note: Stratified row bootstrap of the test period: fraud and legitimate rows are resampled separately so every replicate keeps the observed fraud count. It reflects sampling noise in which test rows were observed, for a fixed trained model and threshold. It does NOT capture time dependence, drift, threshold-selection or retraining variability; see the temporal backtest for that.

block_ci.note: Moving-block bootstrap over simulation steps: contiguous blocks of whole steps are resampled, so transactions from the same hour (and neighbouring hours) stay together. This keeps short-range time dependence that the row bootstrap destroys, and the fraud count varies between replicates. Like the row bootstrap it is conditional on the fitted model and the already-chosen thresholds. Intervals are estimates, not guarantees: they assume the test period is roughly stationary, cannot reflect drift beyond the test period, and become unreliable with few blocks or few fraud cases (some replicates may contain no fraud, making recall/PR-AUC undefined for them; see n_valid).

calibration.note: Calibration asks whether a score of 0.2 means about 20% of such transactions are fraud. Class-weighted models deliberately inflate fraud scores, so raw scores are expected to be poorly calibrated even when ranking (PR-AUC) is good. A Platt (logistic) calibrator is fit on validation scores only and applied to the test period; it is monotonic, so it does not change rankings, PR-AUC or which transactions fall in the top-K. Under prevalence shift a calibrator fit on one period will be miscalibrated on another. With rare fraud, almost all rows sit in the lowest equal-width bin, so ECE is dominated by that bin and can look small while high-score bins are badly miscalibrated; read the reliability bins, not ECE alone. The 'constant' Brier baseline predicts the validation fraud rate for every row (the only rate known before the test period), so it is itself handicapped when prevalence shifts.

warnings: Backtest uses a sample, not the full dataset.

notes.thresholds: No threshold is universally best. 'Max F1' weights missed fraud and false alerts equally; an alert budget fixes reviewer workload instead. The right choice depends on the relative cost of a missed fraud versus a false alert and on review capacity. All thresholds are chosen on validation data; test labels are never used for tuning.

notes.drift: Four different things can change over time: (1) prevalence shift — the fraud rate itself changes, which moves precision and the PR-AUC baseline even for an unchanged model; (2) ranking quality — whether fraud still scores above legitimate transactions (PR-AUC relative to its baseline, ROC-AUC); (3) calibration — whether score values match observed fraud rates (Brier, reliability); (4) threshold drift — the same threshold produces a different alert volume because the score distribution moved (PSI, alerts per 1,000). PSI bands (<0.1 small, 0.1–0.25 moderate, >0.25 large) are an industry heuristic, not a test.
notes.calibration: Calibration asks whether a score of 0.2 means about 20% of such transactions are fraud. Class-weighted models deliberately inflate fraud scores, so raw scores are expected to be poorly calibrated even when ranking (PR-AUC) is good. A Platt (logistic) calibrator is fit on validation scores only and applied to the test period; it is monotonic, so it does not change rankings, PR-AUC or which transactions fall in the top-K. notes.windows: Train steps < validation steps < test steps in every window. Variation across windows shows time-related instability that a single split hides. Each window's model is fit on its training period only (no refit).

disclaimer: Synthetic PaySim data; not evidence of real-world performance.
